description: We are a team of Computational Systems students at ZU interested in technology and problem-solving. We are excited to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary: ARES ATLAS is an interactive mission-planning map for future astronauts walking on Mars, like Google Maps for Mars. We processed a real NASA HiRISE elevation model of part of Jezero Crater and combined it with Perseverance’s actual traverse from NASA’s PLACES data. Users explore the terrain in 2D and 3D, view slope and elevation layers, and generate walking routes using a pathfinding algorithm. They can compare a shorter route with a slope-aware route, and an animated astronaut (EVA-01) walks the chosen route. It addresses the challenge by layering data from several NASA missions into one view that helps plan a Marswalk. It matters because crews will need practical, understandable tools to plan safe and scientifically useful surface excursions.
details:
What it does: ARES ATLAS lets a user explore a real part of Jezero Crater (about 6.6 × 14.4 km), select destinations, and generate Marswalk routes between them. It shows elevation and slope-hazard layers, Perseverance’s historical traverse, a mission dashboard (distance, elevation gain and loss, maximum and average slope, estimated walking time, terrain exposure), and an animated astronaut that walks the route. It also has a NASA weather reference panel and a data-sources panel that marks each source as integrated, partial, reference-only or simulated.

How it works: We parsed the 380 MB HiRISE DTM (DTEEC_045994_1985_046060_1985_U01, a PDS3 float32 raster, 14,266 × 6,673 pixels at about 1 m) and checked its projection against its label. We resampled it to a 16 m browser-friendly grid and computed slopes from it. We projected Perseverance PLACES positions into the same coordinate system and checked them against the terrain elevations (median offset about 4 m). Routes are computed with A* over the terrain grid. The Shorter route minimizes distance. The Safer route adds penalties for steep slopes and for cells near gaps in the data. Both avoid no-data areas.

Benefits: It gives a quick, understandable way to compare route options using real terrain, and it clearly separates real, derived and simulated information.

Goal: A prototype showing how NASA data from several missions can be combined into one planning tool for human explorers.

Limitations: Coverage is one HiRISE terrain model, not the whole crater. The Mars Trek imagery previews were not georeferenced, so the surface is shaded from the elevation data, not satellite imagery. The “safer” route is slope-aware only and does not model dust, radiation, loose soil, ice or weather. The 12 demo destinations, the ice layer, the 2.5 km/h walking speed and the 320 kcal/h energy figure are simulated or assumed and are labeled as such in the app.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js for 3D, HTML canvas for the 2D map, Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Pillow) for data processing, Netlify for hosting.

Use of AI tools: The project concept and requirements were defined by our team, and we used AI tools to help refine and develop it. Claude (Anthropic) helped write the application code and the data-processing script, and helped draft this description and our presentation slides. We also used AI tools to help research and understand the NASA data resources. All NASA data was processed and checked using the files we downloaded from NASA.
